title: Why Do Prime Squares Always Leave 1? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

lines: Pick any prime number bigger than three. Square it, then add seventeen.
Now divide by twelve. <short pause> The remainder is ALWAYS the same! But why?
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's crack this one together.
Here's the question.
Let p be a prime greater than three.
What is the remainder when p squared plus seventeen is divided by twelve?
Is it zero, one, five, six, or eleven?
A prime has exactly two factors, one and itself. Like five, seven, eleven and thirteen.
The remainder is what's left after taking out all the twelves. Twenty-six leaves two.
We don't know p. So the answer must work for EVERY prime bigger than three.
Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
Welcome back! Our first strategy: try a few primes, and look for a pattern.
Start with five. Five squared is twenty-five. Plus seventeen is forty-two.
That's three twelves, plus six.
Next, seven. Seven squared is forty-nine. Plus seventeen is sixty-six.
That's five twelves, plus six. Six again!
Eleven squared is one hundred twenty-one. Plus seventeen is one hundred thirty-eight.
That's eleven groups of twelve, plus six.
Thirteen squared is one hundred sixty-nine. Plus seventeen is one hundred eighty-six.
That's fifteen groups of twelve, plus six.
Six every time! So the answer is D.
Testing is a smart contest shortcut. But it isn't a proof. So WHY is it always six?
Here's another way. Let's write the numbers in rows of six.
A prime bigger than three isn't even, or two would divide it. Cross out columns two, four and six.
It isn't a multiple of three either. Cross out column three.
Only columns one and five are left. Every prime bigger than three lands in them!
Not every number there is prime, like twenty-five. But every prime past three is there.
That's why the question says bigger than three. Two and three got crossed out.
Column one is one after a multiple of six. Column five is one before.
So p is always one away from a multiple of six. Now let's look at p squared.
Take seven. Seven squared is forty-nine dots, in a seven by seven square.
Take away one corner dot. Then move the rest of the bottom row to the side.
Now it's a rectangle: six rows by eight columns. That's forty-eight!
Six and eight are the neighbors of seven, one below and one above.
This works for every p. p squared minus one equals p minus one, times p plus one.
One neighbor is a multiple of six. And p is odd, so the other neighbor is even.
A multiple of six, times an even number, is a multiple of twelve!
So p squared is always a multiple of twelve, plus one. Seventeen is twelve plus five.
One plus five is six. The answer is six, for EVERY prime bigger than three!
When would you pick this way? When you need to be sure a pattern never breaks.
Now, let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
One is the remainder of p squared alone. It forgets the seventeen.
Five is the remainder of seventeen alone. It forgets p squared.
Zero is what seven gives if you forget to square. Seven plus seventeen is twenty-four, two twelves.
Eleven is the biggest remainder twelve allows. But we just showed it's always six.
So here's a great habit. Find each part's remainder, add them, and take out any extra group of twelve.
Ready for a challenge? p is still a prime bigger than three.
What is the remainder when five times p squared, plus nine, is divided by twelve?
Use the same plan. Pause the video, and go for it!
Let's check. p squared is a multiple of twelve, plus one.
Five copies of that make a multiple of twelve, plus five.
Five plus nine is fourteen. That's one more twelve, plus two. So the remainder is two!
Let's test with five. Five times twenty-five, plus nine, is one hundred thirty-four.
That's eleven groups of twelve, plus two. It matches!
If you found a remainder of two, amazing work!
Here's the big idea. Every prime bigger than three is one away from a multiple of six.
So its square always leaves one when divided by twelve. Use that, then add the rest.
I'm Vantee. Keep asking why, and I'll see you next time!
